data.title: Investors Accuse Jefferies, Pershing of Facilitating Massive Fraud in South America — Barrons.com
data.description:
By Kenneth Corbin

A group of 20 investors who say they fell victim to a massive investment fraud are accusing Jefferies and Pershing of failing to take adequate measures to protect them from an unscrupulous South American broker. The investors have filed an arbitration claim against the brokerages, alleging that the central figure in the matter, Sara Goldring, cost them about $16 million in losses. Through a lawyer, she declined to comment.

Goldring, a resident and citizen of Uruguay, controlled two brokerage firms in that country called Custodia de Valores Mobiliarios Corredor de Bolsa, or CVM, and United Brokers, according to a statement of claim filed in an arbitration forum convened by Finra, the brokerage industry's self-regulatory organization.

The claimants accuse Jefferies and Pershing of giving Goldring and her firm "free and unfettered" access to manage clients' money on their platforms, providing a "safe haven" for fraudulent activity that allegedly included churning, cherry-picking, and mismanagement of clients' funds.

For instance, they claim that a Jefferies representative would ask which account to allocate a trade to after it had already been executed, "confirming that Goldring decided which client would bear a position only once its outcome was under way." The claimants say that the trading activity at CVM involved a risky put-options strategy that incurred substantial losses in 2021 and 2022.

A spokeswoman for BNY, Pershing's parent company, acknowledged the arbitration claim but says that the firm hasn't had a chance to review it. "We are aware that claims have been filed but have not received the filing," the spokeswoman says. "We take any allegation of fraud extremely seriously and are committed to conducting a full investigation when we receive the filing."

A spokesman for Jefferies didn't provide a comment on the matter.

Goldring recently pleaded guilty to misappropriation in Uruguay, receiving a two-year sentence of probation, according to media reports and the statement of claim in the Finra proceeding. In the plea agreement, prosecutors said that Goldring used clients' funds for unintended purposes, but didn't pocket money for herself.

$100 million total. Lawyers for the claimants in the case against Jefferies and Pershing allege that Goldring "fraudulently mismanaged" the accounts of more than 700 clients, many of whom were retirees, in Uruguay, Argentina, and Brazil. They peg total losses for all of Goldring's clients at around $100 million.

"This is the next chapter for Goldring's victims," says David Centner, a partner at the law firm Peiffer Wolf, which is representing the claimants. "They have experienced catastrophic losses that have turned their lives upside down, and we aim to prove it wouldn't have been possible without the involvement of the U.S. brokerage and clearing firms Jefferies and Pershing.

Jefferies served as the U.S. introducing broker for Goldring's clients' accounts, with Pershing serving as Jefferies' clearing firm, according to the statement of claim.

That document alleges that the two U.S. brokerage firms ignored numerous red flags that should have alerted them to fraudulent activity and led them to protect investors' funds, including suspicious deposits, trading activity, and the movement of money across accounts.

It describes the claimants as conservative investors with a low-to-moderate tolerance for risk and principal losses. Goldring's brokerage firm allegedly altered these aspects of their investor profiles, including by forging signatures, to accommodate more risk, exploiting weaknesses in Jefferies' and Pershing's systems.

"CVM fabricated hundreds of documents and signatures and grossly misrepresented key details about its customers," the investors allege. "CVM personnel routinely altered signed client documents after the fact to change clients' recorded risk profiles from conservative to aggressive," according to the statement of claim, which says that around 80% of CVM's clients were listed as having an "aggressive" profile.

Goldring's activity has given rise to multiple legal proceedings, including a 2022 appeal by the Central Bank of Uruguay asking Jefferies to pause disbursements from accounts belonging to her and her family members. Jefferies froze the accounts.

Her plea agreement in Uruguay included the forfeiture of $6.8 million held in the United States. In the arbitration case, the claimants are seeking unspecified compensatory and punitive damages, interest, legal fees, and other relief.

data.title: Son of ex-CIA chief Brennan charged over sexual images of minor girls
data.description:
Key points:
  • Complaint alleges FBI phone review found 88 suspected child pornography images
  • Complaint says investigation began in 2024 after tip to child protection group
  • Virginia authorities searched Kyle Brennan's home in July 2024, complaint says

By Jana Winter and Andrew Goudsward

The son of former CIA Director John Brennan was charged on Friday with "transportation of child pornography," according to court documents and a US law enforcement official.

Kyle Brennan, of Warrenton, Virginia, was charged after an FBI review of his cellphone found 88 images that appeared to depict minor girls engaged in sexually explicit conduct, according to a criminal complaint filed in US District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia.

John Brennan is a longtime antagonist of President Donald Trump, and the Justice Department has been investigating the former CIA director for more than a year.

A criminal complaint showed the investigation into Kyle Brennan began independently of the probe into his father, which has been dubbed by both proponents and detractors the “grand conspiracy” probe.

The complaint said the investigation into the younger Brennan originated in 2024 with a tip to the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children, a child protection organization.

Virginia authorities searched his home in July 2024, and the case was referred to the FBI last month, according to the criminal complaint.

Kyle Brennan was under arrest, and it was not immediately clear if he was represented by an attorney.

John Brennan, who led the CIA during Democratic President Barack Obama’s administration, has been scrutinized as part of a wider probe examining whether law enforcement and intelligence officials violated Trump’s civil rights in prior investigations of the president.

The conspiracy investigation has stalled in recent weeks following the resignations of senior prosecutors who had been overseeing it. No charges have so far been brought.

John Brennan has denied wrongdoing and his lawyers have accused prosecutors of improperly targeting Brennan at Trump’s direction.

The former CIA director was subpoenaed to testify before a grand jury last month, but his appearance was postponed after Joseph diGenova, a DOJ official who had been leading the investigation, resigned in September.

data.title: Wheat Futures Recover on Russia-Ukraine Strife — Daily Grain Highlights
data.description:
By Anthony Harrup

  • Wheat for December delivery rose 1.5% on the Chicago Board of Trade Friday to $5.93 1/4 a bushel as Russia and Ukraine continue strikes after this week's talks failed to produce an agreement to ease Black Sea tensions.
  • Soybeans for January delivery rose 1% to $12.31 1/2 a bushel.
  • Corn for December delivery rose 0.7% to $4.45 1/2 a bushel.

HIGHLIGHTS

Bouncing Back: Wheat futures rebound back from the previous day's losses as Russia and Ukraine step up strikes, with no deal seen to ease Black Sea shipping. Brazil cut its 2026 wheat production estimate to 5.3 million metric tons from 5.7 million tons, while Argentina's Rosario exchange raised its wheat forecast for the country to 24.3 million tons from 23.8 million tons.

Mixed Export Sales: The USDA reported corn export sales of 3.48 million metric tons for last week, including a marketing-year high 2.88 million tons for 2026/27 and 594,400 tons for 2027/28. Soybean sales fell 21% from the week before to 1.15 million tons for 2026/27, with an additional 11,200 tons sold for 2027/28. Wheat export sales fell 66% from the previous week to 182,800 tons, a marketing-year low.

Flash Sales: Private exporters reported sales of 303,300 metric tons of corn to Mexico--272,820 tons for the 2026/27 marketing year and 30,480 tons for 2027/28, the USDA said. In addition, soybean sales for 2026/27 included 134,000 tons to China, 120,000 tons to Vietnam and 100,000 tons to unknown destinations

INSIGHT

More Please: Last week's U.S. corn export sales, equivalent to 113.4 million bushels for 2026/27, were the largest for any week since January and the most on record for the comparable week, said Mike Castle of StoneX. "These are the kind of weeks corn bulls need to see help the weak 2026/27 cumulative sales pace play catch-up." Export sales are still lagging last year by 27.8%, Castle added in a note.

Steady Outlook: Brazilian national supply company Conab held its estimate for the 2026/27 soybean harvest at 181.6 million metric tons, with planting 66.8% complete as of the first week of November. Initial development has been generally positive, but conditions have varied across regions, the state company said. "Irregular rainfall, combined with high temperatures and the effects of the El Niño phenomenon at the start of this cycle, calls for a cautious outlook regarding productive potential." Conab sees corn production from its three harvests reaching 148 million tons, also unchanged from October, with higher planted area compared with last year partially offset by lower yields.

AHEAD

  • Tyson Foods Inc. will release its 4Q 2026 earnings report before the market opens Monday.
  • The USDA will release its weekly Grain Export Inspections report at 11 a.m. ET Monday.
  • The USDA will release its weekly Crop Progress report at 4 p.m. ET Monday.
  • The EIA will release its Weekly Petroleum Status Update report at 10"30 a.m. Wednesday

data.title: SpaceX to launch 15th Starship flight, seeking to achieve unprecedented round trip
data.description:
Key points:
  • SpaceX to attempt first catch of Starship's spacecraft on flight planned for Friday
  • Test is key to Musk's bid to make a fully reusable rocket
  • FAA launch license still pending as of Friday morning

By Joey Roulette

SpaceX's latest Starship flight planned for Friday will include its first attempt to catch the spacecraft on a return landing at its Texas launch site, rather than discarding the vehicle at sea, a key test of Elon Musk’s bid to produce a fully reusable rocket system.

The 407-foot-tall (124 m) Starship rocket was scheduled to launch at 4:45 p.m. CT (2245 GMT) from SpaceX's Starbase facilities in South Texas for its 15th flight since 2023 and the second to carry a batch of operational Starlink satellites to orbit. That makes the mission both a revenue-generating endeavor for its satellite-connectivity business and a high-stakes test for a next-generation rocketship still under development.

SpaceX secured its launch license from the Federal Aviation Administration for the Starship flight hours before its planned liftoff, clearing the final regulatory hurdle for the mission.

Musk's colossal space and AI business views Starship as crucial to expanding its network of Starlink internet satellites and, in the future, deploying a vast swarm of AI data-processing satellites dubbed Starmind, as the company increasingly positions itself as a high-tech infrastructure giant.

SpaceX last launched Starship in September, taking the rocket and a payload of satellites to orbit for the first time despite some rocket engines shutting down mid-flight. That mission, planned to last 10 hours, ended after roughly three hours with an intact upper-stage splash-down in the Pacific Ocean.

For Friday's mission, the company expects that Starship's lower-stage Super Heavy booster rocket and its upper-stage crew and cargo vessel will return to the spacecraft's Texas launch site for safe landing and recovery. Plans call for the upper stage to touch down about 22 hours after launch. SpaceX has said it would be a "breakthrough moment in making Starship a reliable, rapidly reusable rocket" if that feat is achieved.

MAKING WAY FOR STARSHIP

SpaceX has previously returned the 236-foot-tall Super Heavy booster three times to its launchpad after sending Starship to space, with the booster flying itself back to Earth minutes after launch and gently descending upright into the grasp of a pair of large mechanical arms fixed to the launch tower. The last such "tower catch" was in March 2025.

For the 15th mission, SpaceX will need to move the Super Heavy booster off the launchpad to make way for Starship, which is expected to descend from space after completing 14 orbits around Earth. That sets up the debut Starship catch to occur at around 2:45 p.m. CT (2045 GMT) on Saturday.

Musk has said he expects to enter a weekly cadence of Starship launches by the first half of 2027, while SpaceX has said it could begin launching Starship from a new Florida launchpad by the end of 2026.

NASA has helped fund Starship's development with roughly $3.2 billion delivered to SpaceX since selecting the rocket in 2021 to serve as a moon lander for its astronauts under the multibillion-dollar US Artemis moon program. SpaceX has put at least $15 billion of its own funds into the rocket's development.

NASA and SpaceX expect Starship to land humans on the moon by 2028, though several major testing milestones remain that analysts and industry engineers believe will push that timeline back. Those milestones include demonstrating complex fuel transfers between Starship "tanker" rockets in orbit, a key process that will enable Starship to travel beyond Earth's orbit to the moon.

Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin is also developing a moon lander, Blue Moon, for NASA under the Artemis program. Blue Moon is poised to join Starship and another spacecraft, NASA's Orion capsule, in Earth's orbit next year for Artemis III, a docking test mission before NASA's planned moon landing missions begin with Artemis IV.

data.title: 4 Takeaways From Dario Amodei's Anthropic IPO Chat With Jamie Dimon — Barrons.com
data.description:
By Nate Wolf

Dario Amodei and Jamie Dimon don't have much in common at first glance, but the two are partners in perhaps the most anticipated capital-market event of the year.

Amodei, the chief executive of Anthropic, sat down with the JPMorgan Chase CEO on Friday for a livestreamed conversation — part of the roadshow for Anthropic's initial public offering, which is expected to happen next week. JPMorgan is one of the IPO underwriters charged with selling shares in the artificial-intelligence lab.

The contrast was evident. Dimon, the blue-blooded East Coast executive from one of humanity's oldest industries, tossed softball questions to Amodei, the Bay Area physicist who helped usher in the AI revolution.

JPMorgan should have no trouble selling Anthropic. The company's $1.4 trillion target valuation is much lower than the $2 trillion analysts had expected earlier this year. Demand for shares is six times higher than supply, Bloomberg reported Thursday, citing sources familiar with the matter.

Apparently there is capital left over after SpaceX's record-shattering IPO in June. "It's almost a clone of SpaceX," Drew Freides, a UBS private wealth advisor, told Barron's. "Same people, same interest."

Amodei and Dimon didn't give any indications about final IPO pricing on Friday, but they did outline some of the opportunities and pain points that could dictate where the stock goes once it begins trading.

"Very Paranoid"

Anthropic has said repeatedly that it will sometimes put the public interest ahead of immediate shareholder value. Amodei echoed that again Friday, arguing the company's culture is its greatest differentiator.

Amodei confirmed that the company turns down applicants who are technically capable but aren't "oriented toward the public benefit." The practice can cause short-term pain, he said, but it appears to pay off: As of Sept. 30, Anthropic earned $6.6 million in revenue per worker over the last year.

The great unknown is what happens if profit and public good collide when Anthropic shares are public. The company has openly called for a slowdown in AI model development, for instance, to prevent uncontrolled AI agents or abuse by bad actors.

"These agents are getting incredibly capable incredibly quickly," Amodei said Friday. "We're very paranoid."

Is $900 Billion Worth of Compute Too Little?

Investors have paid plenty of attention to Anthropic's roughly $900 billion in purchase commitments for chips and data-center capacity. Amodei argued Friday that the $900 billion is, if anything, a conservative outlay.

Anthropic's rapid revenue growth means it has little idea how much money it will earn next year, Amodei said. In turn, that uncertainty makes it difficult to plan compute purchases, which often happen a year or two before Anthropic actually uses the capacity.

The company's 86% gross margins on serving customers — that doesn't include training new models — provide some cushion, as does its $132 billion in cash and other liquid reserves.

Even so, Amodei said Anthropic tends to err on the low side for how much data-center capacity it will need, arguing it can buy more expensive compute on the open market when in a pinch. A $5 billion short-term purchase swung Anthropic to an operating loss last quarter.

Still Shaky on Commoditization

If compute supply is the biggest internal challenge facing Anthropic, the risk of AI models becoming easily replicable commodities is the biggest outside challenge.

The Anthropic CEO didn't directly address the threat of Chinese open-weight models, which companies can run on their own hardware or through cloud providers at a fraction of the cost of Anthropic's most advanced models. For many tasks, cheaper models are sufficient.

Amodei's message was essentially that the best defense is a good offense. As other labs' chatbots caught up to Anthropic's Claude, the company started to focus on new coding tools. Now, as coding starts to mature, Anthropic will put more emphasis on new tools for life sciences, robotics, and cybersecurity, Amodei said: "We're always focused on the frontier."

The one defensive tactic Amodei outlined is using its advanced models to produce relatively cost-efficient, small models that are better than the competition's. Given Anthropic has succeeded so far by competing on quality, not price, this strategy may have its limits.

No Sign of A Delay

It appears Anthropic's IPO will proceed next week as planned, even as the AI trade tries to shake off the turmoil of the midterm elections and Jensen Huang's resignation as Nvidia CEO.

Amodei said Anthropic is looking for public investment because the more cash the company has on hand, the more easily it can invest in AI's next advancements. He isn't concerned about the kind of market environment in which Anthropic is going public.

"We want to underpromise and overdeliver," Amodei said repeatedly, perhaps presaging a first-day pop for investors fortunate enough to get a piece of the IPO.

Write to Nate Wolf at nate.wolf@barrons.com

data.title: H&R REIT breakup plan falls short in unitholder vote
data.description:
Canada's H&R Real Estate Investment Trust said on Friday its unitholders voted against a previously announced C$6.7 billion ($4.7 billion) breakup deal.

The deal, announced in August, was meant to close a multi-year effort to simplify H&R's portfolio and sharpen its focus on residential real estate.

  • H&R had agreed to the breakup deal, under which GO Residential REIT was to acquire its residential portfolio in the US, while a group including Blackstone and entities tied to H&R CEO Tom Hofstedter would buy the other assets

  • Unitholders rejected the deal at a special meeting on Friday, prompting H&R to terminate the arrangement with immediate effect

  • GO Residential said on Friday it would seek a termination fee of C$102.13 million ($71.65 million), adding it was "disappointed" by the meeting's outcome

  • No termination fee would be payable to the consortium, H&R said

  • H&R will also back away from a proposed purchase of a 70% interest in two joint venture development properties owned by Lantower Residential Real Estate Development Trust that it announced in October

  • The company plans to reinstate monthly distributions, pursue asset sales and begin a board rejig that would include CEO succession planning

Subsequent changes in holdings or intentions must be reported in amended filings. This material is from Nov. 5 through Nov. 11, 2026. Source: VerityData

Activist Filings

Vail Resorts (MTN) DKR Oasis Management raised its stake in the mountain resort operator to 3,429,033 shares. Oasis did so through the purchase of 207,858 Vail Resorts shares from Sept. 29 through Oct. 9 at per share prices ranging from $135.10 to $146.

On Oct. 30, Oasis withdrew its nominations of Bryce Roberts and retired Olympic athlete Picabo Street, narrowing its slate of director nominees to former Walt Disney CEO Robert Chapek and M. Ashton Hudson. In a Nov. 2 letter urging shareholders to elect the pair, Oasis pointed to a more than 50% decline in the share price over the past five years, a 15% drop in North American skier visits last season against an industry decline of 10%, and roughly 12% lower pass unit sales for the upcoming season.

Oasis also outlined initiatives including new pass and ticket offerings, better food and beverage value, expanded year-round use of the company's mountains, modernized marketing, a stronger loyalty program, and upgraded technology.

Following the latest purchases, Oasis owns a 9.6% stake in Vail Resorts' outstanding stock. Shares of Vail Resorts have gained roughly 15.3% in value in 2026.

Increases in Holdings

Metalla Royalty (MTA) Tether Holdings raised its stake in the precious-metals royalty and streaming company to 13,663,050 shares. Tether Holdings did so through the purchase of 453,874 Metalla Royalty shares from Oct. 26 through Nov. 4 at per share prices ranging from $7.20 to $7.73. Following the latest purchases, Tether Holdings owns a 14.6% stake in Metalla Royalty's outstanding stock. Shares of Metalla Royalty have remained mostly flat in 2026.

Decreases in Holdings

Vir Biotechnology (VIR) ARCH Venture Partners lowered its stake in the clinical-stage biopharmaceutical company to 12,508,029 shares. ARCH Venture Partners did so through the sale of 796,175 Vir Biotechnology shares from Nov. 3 through Nov. 5 at per share prices ranging from $10.98 to $12.16. Following the latest sales, ARCH Venture Partners continues to own a 7.3% stake in Vir Biotechnology's outstanding stock. Shares of Vir Biotechnology have gained roughly 121% in value in 2026.

Metropolitan Bank Holding (MCB) Patriot Financial Partners lowered its stake in the commercial bank holding company to 584,946 shares. Patriot Financial Partners did so through the sale of 79,938 Metropolitan Bank Holding shares from Oct. 27 through Nov. 5 at per share prices ranging from $98 to $98.10. Following the latest sales, Patriot Financial Partners continues to own a 4.8% stake in Metropolitan Bank Holding's outstanding stock, placing Patriot Financial Partners below the 5% threshold that would require it to report further sales. Shares of Metropolitan Bank Holding have gained approximately 25.4% in value in 2026.

data.title: Measles cases rise to over 5,400 across US
data.description:
Key points:
  • The number of confirmed measles cases in the US has topped 5,400 to 5,412, the CDC said on Friday.
  • Cases have been reported in 45 states and the District of Columbia. Pennsylvania remains the hardest hit, with 1,542 cases as of Friday, according to data from the Pennsylvania Department of Health. The state has also reported seven measles-associated deaths.
  • Earlier this month, New York recorded its first measles-linked death in more than three decades. 
  • The CDC has officially recognized six measles-related deaths. In 2025, the agency said there were a total of three measles-related fatalities.
  • Measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccines are manufactured primarily by Merck () and GlaxoSmithKline ().
